ContRing.description: The Retinotopy protocols on IBC include classic retinotopic paradigms, namely the Wedge and the Ring tasks. The **Contracting Ring** task consists of visual stimuli depicting a thick, contracting ring. The phase of the periodic response at the contraction frequency, measured at each voxel, corresponds to the assessment of the perimetric parameters related to eccentricity (`Sereno et al., 1995 <https://doi.org/10.1126/science.7754376>`__). Under IBC, one run was dedicated to this task (*ap* phase-encoding direction), which was five-and-a-half minutes long. A point was displayed at the center of the visual stimulus in order to keep constant the perimetric origin in all participants. Participants were thus to fixate continuously this point whose color flickered between red, green, blue and yellow throughout the entire run. To keep the participants engaged in the task, they were instructed that after the run, they would be asked which color had most often been presented. Additionally, ten seconds of a non-flickering, red fixation cross were displayed at the end of the run.

condition_descriptions.foveal: During the Contracting Ring task, a thick ring stimulus contracts periodically from the periphery toward the center of the visual field. The foveal condition corresponds to the phase of the contraction cycle at which the ring passes through the innermost eccentricity (the fovea), i.e., the region immediately surrounding the central fixation point. Participants continuously fixate a central point whose color flickers among red, green, blue, and yellow throughout the run. The BOLD response at voxels representing the fovea is characterized by a specific phase relative to the contraction frequency, encoding the foveal eccentricity. The condition is defined against a non-flickering red fixation cross displayed at the end of the run.
condition_descriptions.middle: During the Contracting Ring task, a thick ring stimulus contracts periodically from the periphery toward the center of the visual field. The middle condition corresponds to the phase of the contraction cycle at which the ring passes through the mid-peripheral eccentricity of the visual field. Participants continuously fixate a central point whose color flickers among red, green, blue, and yellow throughout the run. The BOLD response at voxels representing the mid-periphery is characterized by a phase intermediate between the peripheral and foveal phases of the contraction cycle, encoding the mid-peripheral eccentricity. The condition is defined against a non-flickering red fixation cross displayed at the end of the run.
condition_descriptions.peripheral: During the Contracting Ring task, a thick ring stimulus contracts periodically from the periphery toward the center of the visual field. The peripheral condition corresponds to the phase of the contraction cycle at which the ring passes through the far-peripheral eccentricity of the visual field, i.e., the outermost extent of the stimulus. Participants continuously fixate a central point whose color flickers among red, green, blue, and yellow throughout the run. The BOLD response at voxels representing the far periphery is characterized by a phase corresponding to the earliest point in the contraction cycle, encoding the far-peripheral eccentricity. The condition is defined against a non-flickering red fixation cross displayed at the end of the run.

condition_descriptions.foveal: During the Expanding Ring retinotopy run, a thick, dilating ring was presented as the visual stimulus while participants continuously fixated a central point whose color flickered among red, green, blue, and yellow. The 'foveal' condition corresponds to voxels whose periodic BOLD response at the ring-dilation frequency maps to the central (foveal) region of the visual field. The stimulus context includes the color-flickering fixation point; the condition is defined relative to a non-flickering red fixation cross displayed at the end of the run.

Lec2.description: This task belongs to a battery of 8 different localizers that tap on a wide array of cognitive functions provided to us by the `Labex Cortex group <https://labex-cortex.universite-lyon.fr/>`__ at the University of Lyon. Originally described in (`Perrone-Bertolotti et al., 2012 <https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2982-12.2012>`__), this task focuses on silent reading. During the task, participants were presented with two intermixed stories, shown word by word at a rapid rate. One of the stories was written in black (on a gray screen) and the other in white. Consecutive words with the same color formed a meaningful and simple short story in French. Participants were instructed to read the black story to report it at the end of the block, while ignoring the white one. Each block comprised 400 words, with 200 black words (attend condition) and 200 white words (ignore condition) for the two stories. The time sequence of colors within the 400 words series was randomized, so that participants could not predict whether the subsequent word was to be attended or not; however, the randomization was constrained to forbid series of more than three consecutive words with the same color. Data were acquired in two runs, and each word was presented for 100 ms, with a jittered inter-stimulus interval centered around 700 ms.

condition_descriptions.attend: A black word (on a gray screen) is presented for 100 ms with a jittered inter-stimulus interval centered around 700 ms. The word belongs to one of two intermixed stories shown word by word; the black words, when read in sequence, form a meaningful short story in French. The participant is instructed to silently read the black story in order to report it at the end of the block. Each block contains 200 such black words, interleaved with 200 white words from a second story, with the color sequence randomized (no more than three consecutive words of the same color).
condition_descriptions.unattend: A white word (on a gray screen) is presented for 100 ms with a jittered inter-stimulus interval centered around 700 ms. The word belongs to a second story intermixed with the attended black story; the white words, taken in sequence, also form a meaningful short story in French. The participant is instructed to ignore the white story. Each block contains 200 such white words, interleaved with 200 black words, with the color sequence randomized (no more than three consecutive words of the same color).

Audi.description: This task belongs to a battery of 8 different localizers that tap on a wide array of cognitive functions provided to us by the `Labex Cortex group <https://labex-cortex.universite-lyon.fr/>`__ at the University of Lyon. This task was originally described in (`Perrone-Bertolotti et al., 2012 <https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2982-12.2012>`__) together with the `Lec2`_ localizer. Participants listened to sounds of several categories with the instruction that three of them would be presented again at the end of the task, together with three novel sounds and that they should be able to detect previously played items. There were three speech and speech-like categories, including sentences told by a computerized voice in a language familiar to the participant (French) or unfamiliar (Suomi), and reversed speech, originally in French (the same sentences as the "French" category, played backwards). These categories were compared with nonspeech-like human sounds (coughing and yawning), music, environmental sounds, and animal sounds. Participants were instructed to close their eyes while listening to three sounds of each category, with a duration of 12s each, along with three 12 s intervals with no stimulation, serving as a baseline (Silence). Consecutive sounds were separated by a 3 s silent interval. The sequence was pseudorandom, to ensure that two sounds of the same category did not follow each other.

At the end of the task, three previously heard sounds from this category were replayed alongside three novel sounds, and participants were instructed to detect the previously played items.

Visu.description: This task belongs to a battery of 8 different localizers that tap on a wide array of cognitive functions provided to us by the `Labex Cortex group <https://labex-cortex.universite-lyon.fr/>`__ at the University of Lyon. This task, described in (`Vidal et al., 2010 <https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2010.00195>`__), is a visual odd-ball paradigm, in which participants were instructed to press a button (index finger) every time they see a fruit. Images of the target category and other non-target categories were rapidly presented in a pre-randomized order. Stimuli were presented for a duration of 200ms every 1000-1200ms in series of 5 pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods during which patients could freely blink. Each non-target category was presented 50 times during the experiment, and data were acquired in two separated runs.

condition_descriptions.animal: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view images of animals presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. Animal images are a non-target category; no button press is required. Each animal image is presented 50 times across two runs.
condition_descriptions.characters: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view a string of random characters presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. This is a non-target category; no button press is required. Each stimulus is presented 50 times across two runs.
condition_descriptions.face: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view images of human faces presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. Face images are a non-target category; no button press is required. Each face image is presented 50 times across two runs.
condition_descriptions.fruit: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view images of fruits presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. Fruit is the target category: participants are instructed to press a button with the index finger every time a fruit image appears. Data are acquired in two separated runs.
condition_descriptions.house: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view images of houses presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. House images are a non-target category; no button press is required. Each house image is presented 50 times across two runs.
condition_descriptions.pseudoword: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view a string that conforms to a pseudoword presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. This is a non-target category; no button press is required. Each stimulus is presented 50 times across two runs.
condition_descriptions.scene: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view images of naturalistic scenes presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. Scene images are a non-target category; no button press is required. Each scene image is presented 50 times across two runs.
condition_descriptions.scrambled: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view scrambled images presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. Scrambled images serve as a low-level visual baseline for the other stimulus categories. No button press is required.
condition_descriptions.tool: In a visual odd-ball paradigm, participants view images of tools presented for 200 ms every 1000–1200 ms in series of five pictures interleaved by 3-second pause periods. Tool images are a non-target category; no button press is required. Each tool image is presented 50 times across two runs.

Lec1.description: This task belongs to a battery of 8 different localizers that tap on a wide array of cognitive functions provided to us by the `Labex Cortex group <https://labex-cortex.universite-lyon.fr/>`__ at the University of Lyon. This task, described in (`Saignavong et al., 2017 <https://doi.org/10.1142/S0129065717500010>`__), was originally used to test whether brain activity can be detected in single trials with intra-cerebral EEG-fMRI recordings. During the task, participants were presented with three vertically-arranged lines, indicated by the presence of two "+" symbols at both sides, and empty space between them. For each row, a different type of verbal stimuli was presented, and the participant was instructed to make a decision depending on the type of stimuli. The top row presented words, and the decision was an animacy decision ("Is it a living entity?"). The middle row presented pseudowords, and the decision was whether the pseudoword had one or two syllables. Finally, the bottom row presented consonant strings, and participants were instructed to answer if the string was all-uppercase or all-lowercase. First option was selected by pressing with the index finger on the response box whereas second option was given with the middle finger. The trials were presented in blocks, and each block contained a sequence of 5 stimuli for each of the three conditions. The order of this conditions inside each block was randomized across blocks, but fixed for all participants. The "+" symbols for the row corresponding to the next condition turned white to indicate which condition was next. There were two runs with 6 blocks each, each block comprising 15 trials, which were presented for 2000 ms, with an inter-stimulus interval of 500 ms.

condition_descriptions.pseudoword: A pseudoword is presented in the middle row of a three-line display (each row bounded by two "+" symbols). The participant must decide whether the pseudoword has one or two syllables. The first option is selected by pressing the index finger and the second option by pressing the middle finger on a response box. Stimuli are shown for 2000 ms with a 500 ms inter-stimulus interval, in blocks of 5 trials.
condition_descriptions.random_string: A string of consonants is presented in the bottom row of a three-line display (each row bounded by two "+" symbols). The participant must decide whether the string is all-uppercase or all-lowercase. The first option is selected by pressing the index finger and the second option by pressing the middle finger on a response box. Stimuli are shown for 2000 ms with a 500 ms inter-stimulus interval, in blocks of 5 trials.
condition_descriptions.word: A word is presented in the top row of a three-line display (each row bounded by two "+" symbols). The participant must decide whether the word refers to a living entity (animacy decision). The first option is selected by pressing the index finger and the second option by pressing the middle finger on a response box. Stimuli are shown for 2000 ms with a 500 ms inter-stimulus interval, in blocks of 5 trials.

MVEB.description: This task belongs to a battery of 8 different localizers that tap on a wide array of cognitive functions provided to us by the `Labex Cortex group <https://labex-cortex.universite-lyon.fr/>`__ at the University of Lyon. This task, described in (`Hamamé et al., 2012 <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2011.07.087>`__), aims to assess **verbal working memory**. In this case, the participants were presented with a string of 6 characters, from where two, four or six of them can be letters (the rest are "#" symbols). After the string disappears, a single letter appears in screen. The participant had then to indicate if this single letter was part of the previously presented string. This was indicated by the participant with a 5-button response box, with one button for "yes" (index finger) and another for "no" (middle finger). The cognitive load was manipulated with the number of letters, and one condition was included where all the letters of the initial string would be the same one. Each trial commenced with the presentation of a 1500 ms fixation cross, followed by the array of characters (probe) for 1500 ms. After an intermediate period of 3000 ms, and the cue character was presented for 1500 ms. 36 trials were presented in each run. Data were acquired in two separated runs.

condition_descriptions.letters_same: In this condition, the participant is presented with a string of 6 characters in which the letters (two, four, or six of the six positions, the remainder being "#" symbols) are all identical. After the string disappears, a single probe letter is shown, and the participant must indicate whether that letter was part of the previously presented string. Because all letters in the string are the same, the participant effectively needs to maintain only one letter. The trial sequence consists of a 1500 ms fixation cross, a 1500 ms presentation of the character string, a 3000 ms intermediate period, and a 1500 ms presentation of the probe letter. The response is made via a 5-button response box (index finger for "yes," middle finger for "no"). Thirty-six trials are presented per run, across two runs.
condition_descriptions.letters_different: In this condition, the participant is presented with a string of 6 characters in which the letters (two, four, or six of the six positions, the remainder being "#" symbols) are all different from one another. After the string disappears, a single probe letter is shown, and the participant must indicate whether that letter was part of the previously presented string. The trial sequence consists of a 1500 ms fixation cross, a 1500 ms presentation of the character string, a 3000 ms intermediate period, and a 1500 ms presentation of the probe letter. The response is made via a 5-button response box (index finger for "yes," middle finger for "no"). Thirty-six trials are presented per run, across two runs.
condition_descriptions.response: During the response phase, after the probe letter has been displayed, the participant presses a button on a 5-button response box to indicate whether the currently displayed letter was part of the previously presented string: the index finger is used for a "yes" response and the middle finger for a "no" response. This contrasts with a waiting period in which no button press is made.

MVIS.description: This task belongs to a battery of 8 different localizers that tap on a wide array of cognitive functions provided to us by the `Labex Cortex group <https://labex-cortex.universite-lyon.fr/>`__ at the University of Lyon. This task, described in (`Hamamé et al., 2012 <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2011.07.087>`__), and whose name stands for **visuo-spatial working memory** task, consists on a series of events in which the participant will be presented with a 4x4 grid in which two, four or six dots will appear at different positions, after that, the grid would become empty and finally a single dot would appear on it. The participant had then to indicate if this single dot was in the same position than any of the previously presented ones. This was indicated by the participant with a 5-button response box, with one button for "yes" (index finger) and another for "no" (middle finger). The cognitive load was manipulated with the number of dots, and one condition was included where one of the dots would be highlighted, signifying that was the only position to retain. Each trial commenced with the presentation of a 1500 ms fixation cross, followed by the array of dots (probe) for 1500 ms. The empty grid was presented for 3000ms, and the cue dot was presented for 1500 ms. 36 trials were presented on each run. The data were acquired in two runs.

condition_descriptions.dots: In a 4×4 grid, two dots are presented at different positions for 1500 ms, followed by an empty grid for 3000 ms, after which a single probe dot appears for 1500 ms. The participant must retain the positions of both dots in visuo-spatial working memory and subsequently indicate whether the probe dot matches either of the two previously shown positions. No dot is highlighted, so both positions must be maintained.
condition_descriptions.dots_control: In a 4×4 grid, two dots are presented at different positions for 1500 ms, but one of the two dots is highlighted, signifying that only the highlighted position must be retained. After the grid becomes empty for 3000 ms, a single probe dot appears for 1500 ms, and the participant indicates whether it matches the highlighted position. Only one position needs to be maintained.
condition_descriptions.response: Following the probe dot presentation, the participant presses a button on a 5-button response box to indicate whether the single dot currently displayed shares the same location as any of the previously presented dots: the index finger presses the "yes" button and the middle finger presses the "no" button. This condition corresponds to the button-press response phase of the trial.

Moto.description: This task belongs to a battery of 8 different localizers that tap on a wide array of cognitive functions provided to us by the `Labex Cortex group <https://labex-cortex.universite-lyon.fr/>`__ at the University of Lyon. This task is a basic **motor localizer** for several body parts. Participants were presented with three small gray squares over a black background image. At the beginning of each block, a text prompt appeared on screen to indicate which body part would be moved next. Afterwards, the left and right squares turned white to indicate movement of the corresponding side. For example, in the hand condition, participants were required to perform a small movement of the left hand when the left square turned white, and likewise for the right hand. Each block prompted 20 movements, 10 for each side, presented consecutively and in the same order. Two blocks were dedicated to each body part in every run. During each trial, the white squares were presented during 1000 ms, with a 1500 ms interval between trials, resulting in a duration of 25 seconds per block. Each run consisted of 12 blocks, and data were collected over two separate runs.

condition_descriptions.finger_left: Movement of the left index finger, indicated by a button-press. The left of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to tap the left index finger. Each block contains 10 left-finger trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.finger_right: Movement of the right index finger, indicated by a button-press. The right of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to tap the right index finger. Each block contains 10 right-finger trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.foot_left: Movement of the left foot. The left of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to move the left foot. Each block contains 10 left-foot trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.foot_right: Movement of the right foot. The right of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to move the right foot. Each block contains 10 right-foot trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.hand_left: Movement of the left hand. The left of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to perform a small movement of the left hand. Each block contains 10 left-hand trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.hand_right: Movement of the right hand. The right of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to perform a small movement of the right hand. Each block contains 10 right-hand trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.saccade_left: Movement of the eyes to the left. The left of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to shift gaze leftward. Each block contains 10 left-saccade trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.saccade_right: Movement of the eyes to the right. The right of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to shift gaze rightward. Each block contains 10 right-saccade trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.tongue_left: Movement of the tongue to the left. The left of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to move the tongue leftward. Each block contains 10 left-tongue trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.tongue_right: Movement of the tongue to the right. The right of three small squares on a black background turns white for 1000 ms to cue the participant to move the tongue rightward. Each block contains 10 right-tongue trials presented consecutively.
condition_descriptions.instructions: Reading a text prompt displayed on screen at the beginning of each block, indicating which body part will be moved in the subsequent trials. This condition involves visual word recognition and maintenance of the instruction text.

MCSE.description: This task belongs to a battery of 8 different localizers that tap on a wide array of cognitive functions provided to us by the `Labex Cortex group <https://labex-cortex.universite-lyon.fr/>`__ at the University of Lyon. This task described in (`Ossandón et al., 2012 <https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.6048-11.2012>`__) was originally used to study whether visual search processes of a salient target can be thought as a purely bottom-up process, or if it requires action from top-down attentional processes. The task consisted in the presentation of an array of 35 "L" letters, rotated at different angles, together with a target "T" letter (total 36 stimuli in each trial). Subjects were instructed to search for the target and indicate whether it was on the left or right side of the grid, by pressing respectively with the index or middle finger on a 5-button response box. There were two conditions: high-salience (the target is gray while the other stimuli is black) and low-salience (all stimuli are gray). The two conditions were presented alternatively in blocks, with 6 blocks of 10 trials each. Each trial was presented for 3 s with an inter-stimulus interval of 1 s. There was also a 20 s fixation cross between blocks. Data were acquired in two separated runs.

condition_descriptions.high_salience_left: In this condition, an array of 36 stimuli is presented: 35 distractor "L" letters rotated at various angles, rendered in black, together with a single target "T" letter rendered in gray, making it visually salient against the black distractors. The target "T" is positioned on the left side of the grid. The subject searches for the target and indicates its presence by pressing the index finger on a 5-button response box. Each trial lasts 3 s with a 1 s inter-stimulus interval. Trials are grouped in blocks of 10, presented alternately with low-salience blocks, across 6 blocks total.
condition_descriptions.high_salience_right: In this condition, an array of 36 stimuli is presented: 35 distractor "L" letters rotated at various angles, rendered in black, together with a single target "T" letter rendered in gray, making it visually salient against the black distractors. The target "T" is positioned on the right side of the grid. The subject searches for the target and indicates its presence by pressing the middle finger on a 5-button response box. Each trial lasts 3 s with a 1 s inter-stimulus interval. Trials are grouped in blocks of 10, presented alternately with low-salience blocks, across 6 blocks total.
condition_descriptions.low_salience_left: In this condition, an array of 36 stimuli is presented: 35 distractor "L" letters rotated at various angles, together with a single target "T" letter, all rendered in the same gray color, so that the target does not stand out by color from the distractors. The target "T" is positioned on the left side of the grid. The subject searches for the target and indicates its presence by pressing the index finger on a 5-button response box. Each trial lasts 3 s with a 1 s inter-stimulus interval. Trials are grouped in blocks of 10, presented alternately with high-salience blocks, across 6 blocks total.
condition_descriptions.low_salience_right: In this condition, an array of 36 stimuli is presented: 35 distractor "L" letters rotated at various angles, together with a single target "T" letter, all rendered in the same gray color, so that the target does not stand out by color from the distractors. The target "T" is positioned on the right side of the grid. The subject searches for the target and indicates its presence by pressing the middle finger on a 5-button response box. Each trial lasts 3 s with a 1 s inter-stimulus interval. Trials are grouped in blocks of 10, presented alternately with high-salience blocks, across 6 blocks total.

Audio.description:
This task, originally described in (`Santoro et al., 2017 `__), is an auditory localizer. During each run, the participants were presented with sounds from different categories, and were instructed to press a button with the index finger whenever two consecutive sounds were identical. From a group of 288 sounds, divided into 6 different categories, 4 sets were created. Each set contained 72 sounds of each of the categories, and each one was present only in one of the sets. Furthermore, each set was pre-randomized in 3 different orders, and the same sequences were used for all participants. On top of the 72 sounds, each run also included 5 silences and 5 repeated sounds from the original 72. In total, each run consisted of 82 trials of 2 seconds each. It is important to note that the data for this task was acquired using an interrupted acquisition sequence, to minimize the effect that scanner noise can have in the auditory processing targeted by the experiment. To this end, the inter-stimulus interval was programmed in a sequence of 4, 4, and 6 seconds, meaning that the interval between stimuli would be 4s for the first trial, 4s for the second, 6s for the third, and then the sequence repeats until the end of the run. The variability of the ISI and the silence trials avoided stimulus' presentation to be predictable in time. :raw-html:`
` **Note:** We used the MagnaCoil (Magnacoustics) audio device for all subjects except for *subject-08*, for whom we employed Optoacoustics.

condition_descriptions.animal: During this condition, the participant is presented with 2-second auditory stimuli drawn from the animal-sound category within an auditory localizer task. The stimuli are delivered via an in-ear audio device (MagnaCoil/Magnacoustics, or Optoacoustics for one subject) with a variable inter-stimulus interval cycling through 4 s, 4 s, and 6 s. The participant is instructed to press a button with the index finger whenever two consecutive sounds are identical. Each run contains 72 sounds from the category, interspersed with 5 silence trials and 5 repeated sounds, for a total of 82 trials. The specific content or examples of the animal sounds are not detailed in the available evidence.

Attention.description:
This task is a part of a battery of several tasks coming from the `experiment factory `__ published in (`Eisenberg et al., 2017 `__) and presented using `expfactory-python `__ package. The battery was used to capture several aspects of self-regulation, including behavioral inhibition, decision making and planning abilities, among others. The adjustments concerned the translation to all written stimuli and instructions into french, as well as fixing a total time limit for experimentsthat allowed the participants their own pace for responding. All these modifications were done with extreme care of not altering the psychological state that the original tasks were designed to capture during scanning. :raw-html:`
` The Attention is a version of the classical flanker task (`Eriksen and Eriksen, 1974 `__), where the participant has to judge the direction the target flanker (an arrow) is pointing to (left/right). The target flanker is surrounded by other 4 flankers that can be congruent or incongruent with the target one, thus capturing selective attention and inhibitory processes. Two different buttons (index and middle fingers' button, respectively) were assigned to left/right responses, and the participant had to indicate the direction of the central arrow from an horizontal group of 5 arrows. In each trial, one or two positional cues were presented above and below the center of the screen. When one cue was given, the flankers would appear centered around it, whereas when two cues where presented, the flankers would appear centered around one of them. The four flankers surrounding the target would always point to the same direction, and can be congruent or incongruent with the direction the target flanker is facing. The task was acquired in two runs, within the same session as other tasks from the battery and using different phase-encoding directions. :raw-html:`
` For the original version of this task, the authors provide a `simulator `__, which contains the original design.

condition_descriptions.double_congruent: Both positional cues (stars) appear simultaneously above and below the center of the screen, so the participant does not know at which location the arrows will be shown. The four surrounding flankers point in the same direction as the central target arrow (congruent). The participant judges the direction (left or right) of the central arrow using index or middle finger buttons.
condition_descriptions.double_cue: Both positional cues (stars) appear simultaneously above and below the center of the screen, so the participant does not know at which location the arrows will be shown. The flankers appear centered around one of the two cued locations. This is the general double-cue condition, encompassing both congruent and incongruent flanker arrangements.
condition_descriptions.double_incongruent: Both positional cues (stars) appear simultaneously above and below the center of the screen, so the participant does not know at which location the arrows will be shown. The four surrounding flankers point in the opposite direction to the central target arrow (incongruent), acting as distractors. The participant judges the direction (left or right) of the central arrow using index or middle finger buttons.
condition_descriptions.spatial_congruent: A single positional cue (one star) appears, indicating the location at which the arrows will be shown. The four surrounding flankers point in the same direction as the central target arrow (congruent). The participant judges the direction (left or right) of the central arrow using index or middle finger buttons.
condition_descriptions.spatial_cue: A single positional cue (one star) appears, indicating the location at which the arrows will be shown. This is the general spatial-cue condition, encompassing both congruent and incongruent flanker arrangements.
condition_descriptions.spatial_incongruent: A single positional cue (one star) appears, indicating the location at which the arrows will be shown. The four surrounding flankers point in the opposite direction to the central target arrow (incongruent), acting as distractors. The participant judges the direction (left or right) of the central arrow using index or middle finger buttons.

StopSignal.description:
This task is a part of a battery of several tasks coming from the `experiment factory `__ published in (`Eisenberg et al., 2017 `__) and presented using `expfactory-python `__ package. The battery was used to capture several aspects of self-regulation, including behavioral inhibition, decision making and planning abilities, among others. The adjustments concerned the translation to all written stimuli and instructions into french, as well as fixing a total time limit for experimentsthat allowed the participants their own pace for responding. All these modifications were done with extreme care of not altering the psychological state that the original tasks were designed to capture during scanning. StopSignal task was originally used to localize activation relative to inhibition of a prominent motor response (`Bissett and Logan, 2011 `__). :raw-html:`
` Four different polygonal shapes composed the set from which one of them was presented in each trial. Two of them were assigned to the button corresponding to the index finger, and two of them to the button corresponding to the middle finger. The participants were instructed to press the correct button as fast as possible, except if a red-colored star appeared on top of the target stimulus. There were 12 practice trials followed by 123 test trials divided in 3 blocks of 41 trials each, with a resting period of 9 seconds in between blocks. During practice, feedback was provided to indicate correct and incorrect responses, as well as to indicate if the responses were too slow. No stop trials (red star) were present during practice, although the instructions pertaining the red star were presented before practice. This was to build a predominant motor response in order to better capture inhibitory processes. There was a jittered delay between the stop signal and the target stimulus in stop trials that ranged from 400 to 1000 ms. The duration of the stop signal was fixed to 500 ms, the duration of the target stimulus was 850 ms and there was a fixation cross between trials centered around 2250 ms. The task was acquired in two runs, within the same session as other tasks from the battery and using different phase-encoding directions. :raw-html:`
` For the original version of this task, the authors provide a `simulator `__ which contains the original design.

condition_descriptions.go: In go trials, one of four polygonal shapes is presented for 850 ms. Two of the shapes are mapped to the button operated by the index finger and two to the button operated by the middle finger. The participant is instructed to press the button corresponding to the presented shape as quickly as possible. No red star is superimposed on the stimulus. A fixation cross of approximately 2250 ms separates consecutive trials. No stop-signal (red star) trials are included during the 12 practice trials, so that a predominant motor response is established before the test blocks.
condition_descriptions.stop: In stop trials, a polygonal shape (one of the same four shapes used in go trials) is presented for 850 ms, and a red-colored star appears on top of the target stimulus. The red star (stop signal) is displayed for 500 ms and its onset is jittered between 400 and 1000 ms relative to the onset of the target shape. The participant is instructed to withhold the motor response—that is, not to press the button—when the red star is present. The shape stimulus itself is identical to that in go trials; the distinguishing feature is the superimposed red star, which signals that the button press should be held. Stop trials occur only during the 123 test trials (three blocks of 41), not during practice.

TwoByTwo.description:
This task is a part of a battery of several tasks coming from the `Experiment Factory `__ published in (`Eisenberg et al., 2017 `__) and presented using `expfactory-python `__ package. The battery was used to capture several aspects of self-regulation, including behavioral inhibition, decision making and planning abilities, among others. The adjustments concerned the translation to all written stimuli and instructions into french, as well as fixing a total time limit for experimentsthat allowed the participants their own pace for responding. All these modifications were done with extreme care of not altering the psychological state that the original tasks were designed to capture during scanning. :raw-html:`
` TwoByTwo protocol aimed to study the responses to task-switching and cue-switching in every trial, with the aim to asses the activity elicted by switching either or both task and cue, and how switching one affects the response to the other. It consisted of presenting colored single-digit numbers from 1 to 9, preceded by a cue string indicating which task must be performed. For each trail, the task could either be to judge if the number is greater or less than 5; or to judge whether the digit shown is colored in blue or orange. For each of the two tasks, two different strings could be used as cue: for the first, the cue could display either 'Magnitude' or 'High/Low', both strings indicating the participant must judge the quantity; for the second task, the subject could read either 'Color' or 'Orange/Blue' as cues, both strings indicating the task is to judge the color. Two different buttons (index/middle finger) were assigned to the orange/high and blue/low options, respectively. The task is composed by 16 practice trials, followed by 240 trials divided in 3 blocks of 80 trials each. The order of cue and task switching was randomized. The task was acquired in two runs, within the same session as other tasks from the battery and using different phase-encoding directions. :raw-html:`
` For the original version of this task, the authors provide a `simulator `__, it contains a slightly different version of the task in which they switch between three different tasks instead of two.

condition_descriptions.cue_taskstay_cuestay: Cue-presentation phase in which the cue string displayed on screen is identical to the one shown in the immediately preceding trial, meaning both the task (magnitude or color) and the specific cue string (e.g., 'Magnitude' or 'High/Low' for the magnitude task; 'Color' or 'Orange/Blue' for the color task) repeat. The participant is expected to prepare for the same task and respond with the same button mapping (index/middle finger for orange/high vs. blue/low) as in the prior trial.
condition_descriptions.cue_taskstay_cueswitch: Cue-presentation phase in which the task repeats from the previous trial but the cue string changes to the alternative string for that same task. For example, the color task is repeated but the cue switches from 'Color' to 'Orange/Blue', or the magnitude task is repeated but the cue switches from 'Magnitude' to 'High/Low'. The participant must still perform the same task and use the same button mapping, but the cue string itself is different.
condition_descriptions.cue_taskswitch_cuestay: Cue-presentation phase in which the task switches from the previous trial (e.g., from color to magnitude or vice versa) but the cue string presented is the same one that was used for that task in the most recent trial of that task. For example, the task switches from color to magnitude and the cue displayed is the same string that appeared in the previous magnitude trial. The participant must now perform the other task, with the corresponding button mapping (index/middle finger for orange/high vs. blue/low).
condition_descriptions.cue_taskswitch_cueswitch: Cue-presentation phase in which both the task and the cue string switch relative to the previous trial. For example, the task goes from color to magnitude and the cue changes from 'Magnitude' to 'High/Low' compared to the previous magnitude trial. The participant must perform the other task and the cue string is also the alternative one for that task.
condition_descriptions.stim_taskstay_cuestay: Stimulus-presentation phase in which a colored single-digit number (1–9) is displayed on screen after a cue in which both the task and the cue string repeat from the previous trial. The participant judges the digit according to the repeated task (magnitude: greater or less than 5; color: blue or orange) and presses the corresponding button (index or middle finger for orange/high vs. blue/low).
condition_descriptions.stim_taskstay_cueswitch: Stimulus-presentation phase in which a colored single-digit number (1–9) is displayed after a cue in which the task repeats but the cue string switches to the alternative for that task (e.g., 'Color' to 'Orange/Blue'). The participant performs the same task as the previous trial and responds with the appropriate button (index or middle finger for orange/high vs. blue/low).
condition_descriptions.stim_taskswitch_cuestay: Stimulus-presentation phase in which a colored single-digit number (1–9) is displayed after a cue in which the task switches from the previous trial but the cue string is the same one previously used for that task. For example, the task switches from color to magnitude and the cue is the same string as in the prior magnitude trial. The participant must judge the digit according to the new task and press the corresponding button.
condition_descriptions.stim_taskswitch_cueswitch: Stimulus-presentation phase in which a colored single-digit number (1–9) is displayed after a cue in which both the task and the cue string switch relative to the previous trial. For example, the task goes from color to magnitude and the cue changes from 'Magnitude' to 'High/Low' compared to the previous magnitude trial. The participant must judge the digit according to the new task and respond with the appropriate button (index or middle finger for orange/high vs. blue/low).

SelectiveStopSignal.description:
This task is a part of a battery of several tasks coming from the `experiment factory `__ published in (`Eisenberg et al., 2017 `__) and presented using `expfactory-python `__ package. The battery was used to capture several aspects of self-regulation, including behavioral inhibition, decision making and planning abilities, among others. The adjustments concerned the translation to all written stimuli and instructions into french, as well as fixing a total time limit for experimentsthat allowed the participants their own pace for responding. All these modifications were done with extreme care of not altering the psychological state that the original tasks were designed to capture during scanning. :raw-html:`
` Similar to the `StopSignal`_ task, SelectiveStopSignal task required participants to refrain from responding if a red star appears after the target stimulus is presented. In this task, however, the red star only indicates the need to inhibit the motor response in one of the two sides (critical side), while it should be ignored for the other (noncritical side). Motor response is to be given by pressing with the index finger on the corresponding button of the response box. The task is composed by 12 practice trials, followed by 250 test trials divided in 5 blocks of 50 trials each. The task was acquired in two runs, within the same session as other tasks from the battery and using different phase-encoding directions. :raw-html:`
` For the original version of this task, the authors provide a `simulator `__ which contains the original design.

condition_descriptions.go_critical: The participant responds to a visual stimulus on the critical side by pressing the corresponding button with the index finger. The critical side is the one on which a red star (stop signal) appearing after the target stimulus would require the participant to inhibit the motor response. In this condition, the participant executes the response on that side.
condition_descriptions.go_noncritical: The participant responds to a visual stimulus on the noncritical side by pressing the corresponding button with the index finger. The noncritical side is the one on which a red star (stop signal) appearing after the target stimulus should be ignored rather than acted upon. In this condition, the participant executes the response on that side.
condition_descriptions.ignore: A red star (stop signal) appears after the target stimulus on the noncritical side. The participant responds anyway, ignoring the stop signal, and presses the corresponding button with the index finger.
condition_descriptions.stop: A red star (stop signal) appears after the target stimulus on the critical side. The participant withholds the motor response, refraining from pressing the button.

Stroop.description:
This task is a part of a battery of several tasks coming from the `experiment factory `__ published in (`Eisenberg et al., 2017 `__) and presented using `expfactory-python `__ package. The battery was used to capture several aspects of self-regulation, including behavioral inhibition, decision making and planning abilities, among others. The adjustments concerned the translation to all written stimuli and instructions into french, as well as fixing a total time limit for experimentsthat allowed the participants their own pace for responding. All these modifications were done with extreme care of not altering the psychological state that the original tasks were designed to capture during scanning. :raw-html:`
` In this adaptation of the classic Stroop task (`Stroop, 1935 `__), the participants must press one of three buttons depending on the color of the presented word. In contrast to the classic pen and paper version of the task, the congruent and incongruent trials are intermixed. The three words/colors presented were red, green and blue, whose button presses corresponded on the response box respectively to the index, middle and ring fingers. The amount of money and the number of days is different for each trial. :raw-html:`
` For the original version of this task, the authors provide a `simulator `__ which contains the original design.

condition_descriptions.congruent: In this condition, a color word (one of red, green, or blue) is presented on screen printed in the same color as the word it names (e.g., the word "red" displayed in red ink). The participant must press the button corresponding to the color of the word, using the index, middle, or ring finger on a response box mapped to red, green, and blue respectively. Because the word and its ink color match, the instructed color-naming response aligns with the word-reading response. Congruent and incongruent trials are intermixed within the task. The task is presented in French, and participants respond at their own pace within a total time limit.
condition_descriptions.incongruent: In this condition, a color word (one of red, green, or blue) is presented on screen printed in a color that differs from the word it names (e.g., the word "red" displayed in green ink). The participant must press the button corresponding to the ink color of the word, using the index, middle, or ring finger on a response box mapped to red, green, and blue respectively. Because the word and its ink color do not match, the instructed color-naming response diverges from the word-reading response. Congruent and incongruent trials are intermixed within the task. The task is presented in French, and participants respond at their own pace within a total time limit.

ColumbiaCards.description:
This task is a part of a battery of several tasks coming from the `experiment factory `__ published in (`Eisenberg et al., 2017 `__) and presented using `expfactory-python `__ package. The battery was used to capture several aspects of self-regulation, including behavioral inhibition, decision making and planning abilities, among others. The adjustments concerned the translation to all written stimuli and instructions into french, as well as fixing a total time limit for experimentsthat allowed the participants their own pace for responding. All these modifications were done with extreme care of not altering the psychological state that the original tasks were designed to capture during scanning. :raw-html:`
` The ColumbiaCards task is a gambling task in where the participants are presented with a set of cards facing down. In each trial, a different number of cards appear and the participant is informed of the amount gained per good card uncovered, the amount loss when uncovering the bad card, and the number of bad cards in the set. The participant can uncover as many cards as they want, by pressing the index finger's button on the response box, before pressing the middle finger's button to end the trial and start the next one. Uncovering a bad card automatically ends the trial. In each trial, the number of total cards, the number of bad cards, the amount gained per card uncovered and the amount lost if a bad card was uncovered changed. The order in which the cards is pre-determined for each trial, but the participant does not know it. The task is composed by 88 trials divided in 4 blocks of 22 trials each and was acquired in two runs, within the same session as other tasks from the battery and using different phase-encoding directions. :raw-html:`
` For the original version of this task, the authors provide a `simulator `__ which contains the original design.

condition_descriptions.card_flip: In the Columbia Cards gambling task, the card_flip condition corresponds to the participant's action of uncovering (flipping) a face-down card by pressing the index finger's button on the response box. In each trial, a set of cards is presented face-down, and the participant is informed of the amount gained per good card uncovered, the amount lost upon uncovering a bad card, and the number of bad cards in the set. The participant may uncover as many cards as desired before pressing the middle finger's button to end the trial; uncovering a bad card automatically terminates the trial. Across trials, the total number of cards, the number of bad cards, the per-card gain, and the per-bad-card loss vary. The order of cards within a trial is pre-determined but unknown to the participant. The task comprises 88 trials in 4 blocks of 22 trials each, acquired in two runs. The card_flip event is parameterized by the number of loss (bad) cards present in the set, which determines the probability of encountering a bad card on any given flip.

DotPatterns.description:
This task is a part of a battery of several tasks coming from the `experiment factory `__ published in (`Eisenberg et al., 2017 `__) and presented using `expfactory-python `__ package. The battery was used to capture several aspects of self-regulation, including behavioral inhibition, decision making and planning abilities, among others. The adjustments concerned the translation to all written stimuli and instructions into french, as well as fixing a total time limit for experimentsthat allowed the participants their own pace for responding. All these modifications were done with extreme care of not altering the psychological state that the original tasks were designed to capture during scanning. :raw-html:`
` DotPatterns task presents the participant with pairs of stimuli, separated by a fixation cross. The participant has to press a button (index finger) as fast as possible after the presentation of the probe, and only one specific combination of cue-probe is instructed to be responded to differently. This task was designed to capture activation relative to the expectancy of the probe elicited by the correct cue. The task is composed by 160 trials divided in 4 blocks of 40 trials each. Each cue and probe lasted for 500ms, with a fixation cross that separates both lasting for 2000ms. It was acquired in two runs, within the same session as other tasks from the battery and using different phase-encoding directions.

condition_descriptions.correct_cue_correct_probe: In this condition (AX), the participant is presented with a correct cue followed, after a 2000 ms fixation cross, by a correct probe, each lasting 500 ms. This is the target pair of the task. The participant presses a button with the index finger as fast as possible after the probe. The condition captures the response when both the cue and the probe match the instructed pattern, reflecting the expectancy of the probe elicited by the correct cue.
condition_descriptions.correct_cue_incorrect_probe: In this condition (AY), the participant is presented with a correct cue followed, after a 2000 ms fixation cross, by an incorrect probe, each lasting 500 ms. This is a non-target pair. The participant still makes a button response (index finger) after the probe, but the probe does not match the pattern predicted by the correct cue. The condition captures the response when the cue is correct but the probe is not the expected one.
condition_descriptions.cue: In this condition, the participant perceives the cue stimulus, a dot pattern lasting 500 ms. The participant attends to the cue, which precedes a 2000 ms fixation cross and then the probe. The cue may be either correct or incorrect, and its role is to set an expectancy for the subsequent probe. This condition corresponds to the cue-perception period of the trial.
condition_descriptions.incorrect_cue_correct_probe: In this condition (BX), the participant is presented with an incorrect cue followed, after a 2000 ms fixation cross, by a correct probe, each lasting 500 ms. The probe matches the expected pattern, but the preceding cue does not. The participant attends to the probe rather than relying on the cue. The positive label for this condition is 'attend,' distinguishing it from the response-based conditions that follow a correct cue.
condition_descriptions.incorrect_cue_incorrect_probe: In this condition (BY), the participant is presented with an incorrect cue followed, after a 2000 ms fixation cross, by an incorrect probe, each lasting 500 ms. Both the cue and the probe are incorrect. The participant attends to the probe. The positive label for this condition is 'attend,' consistent with the other incorrect-cue conditions in which the participant does not make the instructed button response.

WardAndAllport.description:
This task is a part of a battery of several tasks coming from the `experiment factory `__ published in (`Eisenberg et al., 2017 `__) and presented using `expfactory-python `__ package. The battery was used to capture several aspects of self-regulation, including behavioral inhibition, decision making and planning abilities, among others. The adjustments concerned the translation to all written stimuli and instructions into french, as well as fixing a total time limit for experimentsthat allowed the participants their own pace for responding. All these modifications were done with extreme care of not altering the psychological state that the original tasks were designed to capture during scanning. :raw-html:`
` WardAndAllport task is a digital version of the WATT3 task (`Ward, Allport, 1997 `__, `Shallice, 1982 `__), and its main purpose is to capture activation related to planning abilities. For this, the task uses a factorial manipulation of 2 task parameters: search depth and goal hierarchy. Search depth involves mentally constructing the steps necessary to reach the goal state, and the interdependecy between steps in order to do so. This is expressed by the presence or absence of intermediate movements necessary for an optimal solution of each problem. Goal hierarchy refers to whether the order in which the three balls have to be put in their goal positions can be completely extracted from looking at the goal state or if it requires the participant to integrate information between goal and starting states (which result in unambiguous or partially ambiguous goal states, respectively). Detailed explanations and examples of each one of the four categories can be found in `Kaller et al., 2011 `__. :raw-html:`
` The task was divided in 4 practice trials, followed by 48 test trials divided in 3 blocks of 14 trials each, separated by 10 seconds of resting period. Data was only acquired during the test trials, although the practice trials were also performed inside the scanner with its corresponding equipment. In each trial, the participant would see two configurations of the towers: the test towers on the left, and the target towers on the right. The towers of the right showed the final configuration of balls required to complete the trial. Three buttons were assigned to the left (index finger' button), middle (middle finger's button) and right (ring finger's button) columns respectively, and each button press would either take the upper ball of the selected column or drop the ball in hand at the top of the selected column. On the upper left corner, a gray square with the text "Ball in hand" would show the ball currently in hand. All trials could be solved in 3 movements, considering taking a ball and putting it elsewhere as a single movement. The time between the end of one trial and the beginning of the next one was 1000 ms.

condition_descriptions.planning_ambiguous_direct: Planning phase of the WATT3 tower task with a partially ambiguous goal state (complex goal hierarchy) and no intermediate movements (simple search depth). The participant views a test tower configuration on the left and a target tower configuration on the right, where the order in which the three balls must be placed in their goal positions cannot be fully extracted from the goal state alone and requires integrating information between the goal and starting states. No intermediate movements are necessary for the optimal solution. The participant plans the sequence of button presses (left, middle, or right column buttons) to move balls between columns, with a 'Ball in hand' indicator shown in the upper-left corner. All trials are solvable in three movements.
condition_descriptions.planning_ambiguous_intermediate: Planning phase of the WATT3 tower task with a partially ambiguous goal state (complex goal hierarchy) and intermediate movements (complex search depth). The participant views a test tower configuration on the left and a target tower configuration on the right, where the order of ball placement requires integrating information between the goal and starting states, and intermediate movements are necessary for the optimal solution. The participant plans the sequence of button presses (left, middle, or right column buttons) to move balls between columns, with a 'Ball in hand' indicator shown in the upper-left corner. All trials are solvable in three movements.
condition_descriptions.planning_unambiguous_direct: Planning phase of the WATT3 tower task with an unambiguous goal state (simple goal hierarchy) and no intermediate movements (simple search depth). The participant views a test tower configuration on the left and a target tower configuration on the right, where the order in which the three balls must be placed in their goal positions can be fully extracted from the goal state alone. No intermediate movements are necessary for the optimal solution. The participant plans the sequence of button presses (left, middle, or right column buttons) to move balls between columns, with a 'Ball in hand' indicator shown in the upper-left corner. All trials are solvable in three movements.
condition_descriptions.planning_unambiguous_intermediate: Planning phase of the WATT3 tower task with an unambiguous goal state (simple goal hierarchy) and intermediate movements (complex search depth). The participant views a test tower configuration on the left and a target tower configuration on the right, where the order of ball placement can be fully extracted from the goal state alone, but intermediate movements are necessary for the optimal solution. The participant plans the sequence of button presses (left, middle, or right column buttons) to move balls between columns, with a 'Ball in hand' indicator shown in the upper-left corner. All trials are solvable in three movements.
condition_descriptions.move_ambiguous_direct: Execution (move) phase of the WATT3 tower task with a partially ambiguous goal state (complex goal hierarchy) and no intermediate movements (simple search depth). The participant executes the planned sequence of button presses (left, middle, or right column buttons) to move balls between columns, with a 'Ball in hand' indicator shown in the upper-left corner. BiologicalMotion1.description: The phenomenon known as *biological motion* was first introduced in (`Johansson, 1973 <https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03212378>`__), and consisted in point-light displays arranged and moving in a way that resembled a person moving. The task that we used was originally developed by (`Chang et al., 2018 <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.03.013>`__). During the task, the participants were shown a point-light "walker", and they had to decide if the walker's orientation was to the left or right, by pressing on the response box respectively on the index finger's button or the middle finger's button. The stimuli were divided in 6 different categories: three types of walkers, as well as their reversed versions. The division of the categories focuses on three types of information that the participant can get from the walker: global information, local information and orientation. Global information refers to the general structure of the body and the spatial relationships between its parts. Local information refers to kinematics, speed of the points and mirror-symmetric motion. Please see `Chang et al., 2018 <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.03.013>`__ for more details about the stimuli. The data was acquired in 4 runs. Each run comprises 12 blocks with 8 trials per block. The stimulus duration was 500ms and the inter-stimulus interval 1500ms (total 16s per block). Each of the blocks was followed by a fixation block, that also lasted 16s. Each run contained 4 of the six conditions, repeated 3 times each. There were 2 different types of runs: type 1 and 2. This section refers to run type 1, which contained both global types (natural and inverted) and both local naturals. For run type 2 refer to :ref:`BiologicalMotion2`.

condition_descriptions.global_inverted: A point-light walker in which global structural information (the general body structure and spatial relationships between parts) is preserved, but individual local trajectories are mirror-symmetric. This global walker is inverted (described as 'upside-down' in the condition description; the associated contrast labels it as 'flipped on X axis'). The participant views the stimulus for 500 ms and must judge whether the walker is oriented to the left or to the right, pressing the index-finger button for left and the middle-finger button for right. The stimulus is presented in blocks of 8 trials with a 1500 ms inter-stimulus interval (16 s per block), followed by a 16 s fixation block.
condition_descriptions.global_upright: A point-light walker in which global structural information (the general body structure and spatial relationships between parts) is preserved, while individual local trajectories are mirror-symmetric, rendering local kinematic cues uninformative. This is the 'global-only' condition in the original experiment (Chang et al., 2018). The participant views the stimulus for 500 ms and must judge whether the walker is oriented to the left or to the right, pressing the index-finger button for left and the middle-finger button for right. The stimulus is presented in blocks of 8 trials with a 1500 ms inter-stimulus interval (16 s per block), followed by a 16 s fixation block.
condition_descriptions.natural_inverted: A point-light walker in which local information (kinematics, speed of the points, and mirror-symmetric motion) is preserved, but the points are randomly shuffled along the X-axis, rendering global structural cues uninformative. This local-natural walker is inverted along the horizontal axis (the associated contrast labels it as 'flipped on X axis'). The participant views the stimulus for 500 ms and must judge whether the walker is oriented to the left or to the right, pressing the index-finger button for left and the middle-finger button for right. The stimulus is presented in blocks of 8 trials with a 1500 ms inter-stimulus interval (16 s per block), followed by a 16 s fixation block.
condition_descriptions.natural_upright: A point-light walker in which local information (kinematics, speed of the points, and mirror-symmetric motion) is preserved, but the points are randomly shuffled along the X-axis, rendering global structural cues uninformative. This is the 'local-natural' condition in the original experiment (Chang et al., 2018). The participant views the stimulus for 500 ms and must judge whether the walker is oriented to the left or to the right, pressing the index-finger button for left and the middle-finger button for right. The stimulus is presented in blocks of 8 trials with a 1500 ms inter-stimulus interval (16 s per block), followed by a 16 s fixation block.
